name: Retirement
seoDesc: Retirement: work out retirement age from the current age and the amount already saved. A free finance calculator with the formula, units and a worked example.
summary: Supply the current age, the amount already saved, the investment rate and the total savings and the Retirement calculator solves for retirement age. Think of it as a shortcut for a budget, a loan conversation, a payslip check or a what-if before you talk to a lender. Every field is labelled the way you would say it out loud, so you can usually fill the form from memory and only look up the numbers you genuinely do not know.

sections.title: How does the Retirement calculator work?
sections.html:
The Retirement calculator takes the values in the form, applies the relationship described below and reports retirement age in the results panel.

Working from the top of the form: you choose the option that describes your case (the sex and the country); then you type in the current age, the amount already saved, the investment rate and the total savings (Your savings).

Press Calculate and the page works through the equation with the values you supplied and derives the rest; it then keeps up with you as you correct a typo.

Because the equation can be rearranged for each of its variables, the page also runs backwards. Leave the box you want to know empty, fill in the rest, and it solves for the missing one instead. That is useful when you know the answer you need rather than the inputs you have.

sections.title: The formula behind the Retirement calculator
sections.html:
The page rests on a handful of relationships. Each one can be rearranged for any of its variables, which is what makes the calculator work in both directions:

Savings amount=investment rate × (amount already saved × (investment rate + 1 ^ -current age + retirement age) − total savings) ÷ (1 − (investment rate + 1 ^ -current age + retirement age))
Government pension=(investment rate × total savings + total retirement income × (investment rate + 1 ^ -life expectancy + retirement age) − total retirement income) ÷ ((investment rate + 1 ^ -life expectancy + retirement age) − 1)
Cost of living=(1 ÷ 100) × budget percentage × total retirement income
Cost of living=-money left + total retirement income
Retirement income from savings=-investment rate × total savings ÷ ((investment rate + 1 ^ -life expectancy + retirement age) − 1)
Total savings=(investment rate × amount already saved × (investment rate + 1 ^ -current age + retirement age) + savings amount × (investment rate + 1 ^ -current age + retirement age) − savings amount) ÷ investment rate

Read it as an ordinary equation. Where a word appears instead of a letter, it is the label of one of the boxes in the form; where a function appears, it is the usual mathematical meaning of that function.

If a number looks wrong, check three things in this order: that the units match what you had in mind, that no drop-down is still on its default, and that the value you entered is on the same scale as the rest — a rate typed as 5 rather than 0.05 is the classic mistake. Those three account for almost every answer that is out by a factor.

sections.title: How are units and precision handled?
sections.html:
Units are handled by conversion rather than by convention. Whatever chip you choose, the number is turned into a single base unit before the calculation and rendered back afterwards, so a form filled with a mixture of systems still gives the right answer.

Display rounding is separate from calculation rounding: the digits you see are shortened, the value behind them is not. Numbers far from everyday size are shown in scientific notation so the significant digits stay readable.

sections.title: When should you use it?
sections.html:
The Retirement calculator earns its place in the middle of a task, not instead of one. It is most useful when:

  • Preparing questions for a lender, an accountant or an adviser
  • Comparing two offers that quote their costs in different ways
  • Sizing up a purchase before you commit to it
  • Any time the same 4 figures keep coming back — the current age, the amount already saved and the investment rate — and you would rather not repeat the arithmetic by hand each time.

sections.title: How do you get a reliable answer?
sections.html:
• Write the answer down with its unit. A bare number copied into a report later is exactly where units get lost.
  • Keep the units you enter consistent. Mixing centimetres into a field that expects metres is the single most common way to get an answer that is out by a factor of a hundred.
  • Round only at the end. The calculator carries full precision internally, so re-entering a value you already rounded is the fastest way to introduce drift.
  • If a result surprises you, look at the order of magnitude before the digits: a plausible number in the wrong unit looks more convincing than an implausible one, and is easier to miss.

sections.title: What else is worth knowing?
sections.html:
• Filling in more than one box is fine. The most recently edited field is the one treated as known, so you can switch direction without reloading.
  • Answers that depend on a drop-down reflect the option you picked, not a range. Switching to a neighbouring option is the quickest way to see how much that factor matters.
  • Some options are backed by reference tables that ship with the page, so the values are fixed data rather than a live lookup.
  • Fields that are still blank are exactly the ones the calculator has not yet been given, so the results panel is a reliable map of what is missing.

faq.q: What does the Retirement calculator work out?
faq.a: It returns retirement age, derived from the current age, the amount already saved and the investment rate. Every field in the form feeds the same relationship: press Calculate once and changing any of them updates the result immediately, with no page reload.

faq.q: What do I need to enter to use the Retirement calculator?
faq.a: The form asks for the current age, the amount already saved, the investment rate and the total savings, which is 11 fields in total. Each one is labelled with what it means and, where relevant, the unit it expects. Anything you leave blank is treated as the value to solve for.

faq.q: Can I enter savings amount in a different unit?
faq.a: Yes. Savings amount opens in US Dollar and the chip beside it offers 113 units. The number you typed keeps its magnitude and only its label changes; the calculation itself happens in a common base unit, so mixing systems in one form is safe.
Yes. Each variable in the relationship can be the one being solved for: fill in the answer you are aiming at, leave the field you want empty, and the calculator inverts the equation for you.

faq.q: How much do the drop-down choices change the answer?
faq.a: There are several choices to make (2 in total), and each one selects a different case rather than scaling the result. Switching a single option and watching the result is the fastest way to see how much that choice is worth.

With the values the page starts from, the calculator reports Retirement age = 0. Treat that as a reference point rather than a recommendation: it exists so you can tell at a glance whether your own inputs are on the same scale.

faq.q: Is the Retirement calculator free to use?
faq.a: Yes — no account, no sign-up and no limit on how many times you run it. The arithmetic happens in your browser, so the values you type are not sent anywhere.
